newsitem.title: BOSNIA: West may penalise Bosnia for failure to agree laws.
newsitem.headline: West may penalise Bosnia for failure to agree laws.

text.p: The Bosnian government has failed to pass key laws ahead of a deadline set by Western allies in May and may now face penalties from the international community, officials said on Saturday.

The government which represents Moslems, Serbs and Croats in the divided country, pledged in the Dayton peace accords that ended the Bosnian war in November 1995 that it would pass laws on passports, citizenship and ambassadorial posts, but yet none has been agreed.
Western powers meeting at a NATO summit in Sintra, Portugal, in May, threatened to take action if such problems persisted.
They said that unless Bosnia appointed ambassadors by August 1, representing the new unified government, contact with existing foreign missions would be jeopardised.
The declaration drawn up after the NATO summit also said proposals for laws on citizenship and passports had to be approved speedily by the Bosnian government.
"If the laws were not in place by 1 August 1997, the (international community's) High Representative would recommend action," it read.

Representatives of the five nation Contact Group on the former Yugoslavia -- France, Britain, the United States, Germany and Russia -- met in Sarajevo on Friday to discuss what penalties would be imposed on Sarajevo if agreement were not reached.
Duncan Bullivant, spokesman at the office of the High Representative, told Reuters on Saturday penalties were still possible, though the parties were "pretty close" on the ambassadorial issue.
Members of the Bosnian presidency and government officials met until late on Friday night to try and reach agreement.

High Representative Carlos Westendorp, in charge of implementing civilian aspects of the Dayton peace accord, was to announce later on Saturday whether punitive measures would be taken and what they would consist of.
The dispute over issuing passports is a symbol of the continued division between the Serb Republic and the Moslem-Croat Federation, which constitute post-war Bosnia.
One Bosnian government official said the parties could not agree on whether each of the two halves of Bosnia could issue their own passports, and said the federation did not believe they should.

"It is connected with the issue of citizenship. According to Dayton, there can be three citizenships: Bosnia's state citizenship, and the Federation and Serb Republic entity citizenships," the official said.

Either passports are issued first at state level, granting people Bosnian citizenship and then giving them either federation or Serb republic citizenship, or they are issued first by each entity and then by the state.

Haris Silajdzic, co-chairman of the council of ministers, said the Serbs wanted to grant ethnic Serbs in Croatia citizenship of the Serb Republic which could lead to 150-200,000 Serbs, not originally from Bosnia, gaining Bosnian state citizenship.
Another sticky issue for the government is how to distribute ambassadorial posts to the three ethnic groups.

The government official said Bosnian Croats were posing the biggest problem "because they want ethnic parity in the distribution of posts although they represent only 17 percent of the total population in Bosnia".
All 33 ambassadorial posts are still in dispute.
